disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is characterized by a continuous period of illness during which there is a major depressive episode concurrent with symptoms of schizophrenia, such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized thinking. To meet criteria, there must be at least a two-week period of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms, as well as substantial mood episodes present for the majority of the total duration of the illness. The course is often chronic or relapsing, with functional impairment in work, relationships, or self-care, and it can be difficult to distinguish from major depressive disorder with psychotic features or schizophrenia with secondary mood symptoms. Diagnosis relies on carefully establishing the temporal relationship between psychotic and mood symptoms and ruling out substance-induced or medical causes.

narrative.stressor: Eva’s symptoms began to coalesce in the year after a contentious divorce that upended the life she had been carefully planning around museum work, a stable marriage, and eventual home ownership. Initially, she channeled her hurt into overworking on freelance design projects and elaborate meal-prepping, but as months went by her social circle narrowed, she pulled back from the co-ed soccer league and gallery nights, and she spent more and more time alone in her apartment planning trips and creative projects she never actually started. Subtle changes in her thinking and mood were written off by friends as a reaction to the divorce until she abruptly withdrew from her art-education coordinator training program, missed rent payments despite having savings, and stopped showing up to community workshops she had organized. Nearly two years after the divorce, her ex-husband and a close friend convinced her to see a psychiatrist when she confided that she had quit all her freelance work because she felt that something was deeply wrong with her and that she no longer trusted her own mind.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’ve ruined everything in my life and I don’t deserve to be doing art or working with anyone anymore.”

narrative.stressor: For James, the turning point came when his clinic underwent a major electronic health record upgrade at the same time he enrolled in evening classes toward his LPN and health‑administration goals. What started as his usual busy schedule of long shifts, jogging, and late‑night studying gradually became unsustainable as staffing shortages increased his workload, and he began picking up extra shifts out of a sense of responsibility to his patients. Over the next year and a half, his performance slipped: he missed documentation deadlines, stopped joining basketball games, and abandoned his Raspberry‑Pi projects, telling himself he just needed to "push through" the stress and get to the next certification. He finally sought psychiatric care after his supervisor called him in about repeated errors at intake and he realized that, despite cutting back on everything but work and sleep, he felt increasingly unable to concentrate or trust his own judgment with patients’ information.
narrative.chief_complaint: “No matter how much I rest, I feel completely drained and can’t keep up or focus at work anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Patricia’s difficulties escalated after her husband developed complications from longstanding diabetes, leading to multiple hospitalizations and a sudden shift in her role from partner to primary caregiver. She tried to maintain her boutique and community commitments—farmer’s market stalls, book club, and volunteering at the senior center—while managing his medications and appointments, but over the next year her once‑steady routines began to fray; orders were delayed, the workshop grew disorganized, and she started skipping yoga classes that had long helped her manage anxiety. As the strain mounted, she closed the shop for “redecorating” far more often than she could afford, avoided answering customer messages, and spent more time alone in her garden, unable to finish even simple repair jobs she had done for decades. She eventually came to psychiatric attention after a long‑time client, concerned by repeated cancellations and an uncharacteristically subdued demeanor, gently suggested she talk to her doctor, and her husband echoed the concern when she admitted she no longer felt capable of running the business or facing people at the market.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve lost all interest in my jewelry work and the things I used to love, and I can’t make myself care enough to keep the shop going.”
